title: Krishna's Final Instruction to Uddhava
story:
By the time the Yadava clan had all but destroyed itself, there was almost no one left at Krishna's side. He had watched the course of his own maya run out to its end, and now he walked to the bank of the Sarasvati, sipped the water of the river, and sat down at the foot of an ashvattha tree.

There he told Uddhava to go to Badari, the hermitage in the north. Uddhava, who had followed Krishna his whole life, found that he could not leave his feet. It was not that he defied the command; it was that the road north led away from Krishna, and that was the one road Uddhava had never learned to take. He lingered. He followed at a distance, waiting. And Krishna, who takes away the sorrow of all who surrender to him, found him there and said: I know your heart's desire. I grant you what is hard for others to attain.

Uddhava has left us his own account of that hour. He saw his Lord seated alone, contemplating — the beloved one he had always sought. Krishna was dark and radiant, free of all passion, his eyes peaceful and touched with red, his right foot resting upon his left thigh. He was the refuge of the great devotee, and when Krishna spoke, Uddhava — the great devotee, the friend of Vyasa himself — bowed with joy, his head bent low.

This is the last of your births, Krishna told him. My grace has come to you. What I spoke long ago to Brahma, seated on the lotus born from my navel at the beginning of creation — that is what I give you now.

Uddhava could barely take it in. He had asked for nothing; he had only failed to walk away when he was told to go. And now he was to receive what the Lord had spoken to Brahma at the dawn of the universe. He praised Krishna — the one who acts without desire, whose birth and non-birth alike are beyond telling, the refuge of the distressed, whom the frightened reach by fleeing from every fear; the one who is invoked in mantras, whose knowledge of the self is unbroken, complete, eternal; the one who, knowing the secret of the self, could unfold that knowledge fully. All his life Uddhava had been blessed, moment by moment, by the grace of that Supreme Person, and only now did he understand how much had already been given. To whom else would the Lord teach it, he wondered, but to one whose heart was laid open? For those who serve the lotus of his feet, what could be hard to obtain, even among the four aims of life?

And so, to Uddhava whose heart had been opened, the supreme Lord taught the supreme knowledge — the knowledge that illuminates the secret of the self — and granted him the state that is hard for others to attain.

It was the final teaching, given at the foot of a tree on the bank of a river, to the one man who could not make himself leave Krishna's feet. The world would long remember the words spoken at Kurukshetra; what Uddhava carried away that day was what came after them — the knowledge of the self, granted in a whisper by a river.
reflection: Uddhava is told to go, and his reward is that he cannot; he receives the supreme state not for asking but for refusing to leave Krishna's feet. The episode quietly suggests that the last grace comes to those who cannot bear separation, even when the Lord himself sends them away.
tradition_note: The account in the third canto is Uddhava's own recollection of the moment; the fuller exposition of the teaching he received is traditionally known as the Uddhava Gita.
locations: the foot of an ashvattha tree
next_story_tease: Krishna's grace had one more errand for Uddhava: a message of comfort to the people of Vrindavan.
